content: The study evaluated the consumption of food items either as meals or snacks. The variety of food items consumed was categorized as one type per day, two different types per day, three different types per day, or more than three different types per day. These variations in food variety were also assessed on a weekly basis. The types of milk consumed (breast milk, animal milk, infant formula, or mixed) were also considered. The frequency, variety, and amount of exposure to fruits and vegetables (FV) and nuts, pulses, and seeds (NPS) were compared as follows: Less frequent or less varied consumption of fruits and/or vegetables. Less frequent consumption or lower amounts of nuts, pulses, and/or seeds. The primary outcomes measured included: 1. Subsequent consumption of food items across the two food groups (FV and NPS) at various ages (1 year, 2 years, 3 years, 4 years, 5 years, and beyond). 2. Nutrient intake (e.g., saturated fat, protein, sodium, fiber/phytate, fats) as reported by study authors. 3. Nutrient status at the end of the study, including blood concentrations of vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin D, vitamin E, B vitamins, zinc, iron, folate, selenium, lutein, carotenoids, iodine, fatty acids (omega-3 and omega-6), anemia, and antioxidants. 4. Anthropometric indices as continuous outcomes. 5. Child development, as defined by the study authors. 6. Exposure to contaminants (e.g., aflatoxins), as reported by the study authors. 7. Displacement of other foods or dietary adequacy, as reported by study authors. Secondary outcomes included: 1. Food and taste preferences later in life. 2. Lipid profiles (e.g., total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein, high-density lipoprotein) at the study endpoint or latest follow-up. 3. Inflammatory markers (e.g., C-reactive protein, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1) at the study endpoint or latest follow-up. 4. Gut microbiota and related factors (e.g., Bifidobacterium, Clostridia, short-chain fatty acids, environmental enteric dysfunction, microbiome) at the study endpoint or latest follow-up. 5. Adverse effects, as reported by study authors. 6. Morbidity due to infectious diseases. 7. Foodborne illnesses unrelated to storage and handling. 8. Bone health, as defined by study authors. 9. Oral health, as defined by study authors. 10. Safety concerns (e.g., choking). The GRADE framework was used to rank the eight most critical outcomes for quality of evidence and strength of recommendations. These outcomes included wasting, underweight, stunting, anemia, height-for-age z-scores (HAZ), stability and change in vegetable/fruit consumption, linear growth, and ferritin levels below 20 μg/L. The review included studies from all settings in low-, middle-, and high-income countries. Eligible study designs included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials, cohort studies (prospective and retrospective), cross-sectional studies, and case-control studies. Qualitative studies and reviews were excluded. The search strategy was developed using the PICO methodology and included databases such as MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, African Index Medicus, LILACS, Cochrane CENTRAL, and WHO's eLENA. Grey literature was also searched using Google Scholar and organizational websites (e.g., UNICEF, Nutrition International, Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition, Helen Keller International, CDC). No restrictions were placed on publication date or language. The selection of studies was managed using Covidence software. Four reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts for relevance. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by a fifth reviewer. Data extraction was performed using a standardized Excel form, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by an independent reviewer. The quality of included studies was assessed using tools such as the Cochrane Risk of Bias-2 (ROB-2) tool for RCTs, the NIH tool for observational studies, and the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. The GRADE tool was used to assess the certainty of evidence for selected outcomes, with evidence rated as very low, low, moderate, or high. The review identified 31,124 records, of which 21,609 were screened after removing duplicates. Six studies met the inclusion criteria for the FV/NPS review, involving a total of 23,346 children aged 6 months to 7 years. Frequency of consumption was defined differently across studies, and no studies reported on the variety of FV or the amount of NPS consumption. Four studies were rated as having a high risk of bias, one study as medium risk, and one study as low risk. The main reasons for exclusion of studies were the lack of measurement or reporting of frequency, variety, or amount of consumption. Two ongoing trials were identified as potentially eligible but could not be included due to data limitations. Overall, the review highlights the challenges in synthesizing evidence due to heterogeneity in study designs, outcome metrics, and frequency categories. A narrative synthesis was conducted, as meta-analysis was not feasible. Subgroup analyses by age groups were also not possible due to sparse and heterogeneous data.
